boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Boydton Plank Road record (October 27-28, 1864) in the Richmond-Petersburg Campaign [June 1864-March 1865]. Fair Oaks & Darbytown Road (VA080) is the simultaneous co-operating demonstration north of the James. Humphreys was Meade's chief of staff and directed Warren's crossing in person, so his account is a participant's. Army-wide returns, raid-wide and multi-action loss totals, and the siege as a whole are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force text reads 'Corps (35,000 total)' and the live description 'more than 30,000 men'. Humphreys says the plan was to move 30,000 to 35,000 effective infantry with Gregg's cavalry of about 3,000, that Hancock took about 10,000 and Parke and Warren about 11,000 each after leaving 1,500 and 2,500 in their works, and that the October 20 return gave Hill's three divisions 13,638 and Hampton's cavalry 5,453; he relays Warren's statement that 3,913 of his men had never fired a musket.
claims.rationale: Planned and approximate effective strengths and a Confederate return of October 20, of different populations. None is adopted as a matched opening strength; live zeros are not measured absence.

claims.value: The frozen and live results read Confederate victory; NPS says the Confederates kept the Boydton Plank Road for the winter. Humphreys says Mahone was driven from the field in confusion but Hancock was ordered to withdraw that night; Lee says the enemy retired during the night leaving his wounded and more than 250 dead.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit. Tactical repulse of Mahone and the Union withdrawal are both retained.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 3,058 (1,758 US; 1,300 CS), matching the live field. Humphreys gives Hancock's loss as 857 killed and wounded and 625 missing, Warren's as 211 killed and wounded and 48 missing, the Adjutant General's table as 143 killed, 653 wounded and 488 missing, and judges the Confederate losses at least equal; Lee reports Mahone's 400 prisoners and Hill's total of 700.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. Humphreys' and the table's Union figures differ; Lee's prisoner totals and the Union missing overlap.

open_questions: Hancock's, Warren's, Parke's and Gregg's reports (Volume XLII Nos. 17, 121, 187, 229), Egan's and Mott's reports, Hill's and Hampton's reports (Nos. 372, 374) and the compiled returns remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC (the live NPS page and the frozen Arnold rows) is one family. Humphreys' The Virginia Campaign of ’64 and ’65 (1883) is an interested history by the Army of the Potomac's chief of staff, later commander of its Second Corps, in the same author family as the registered From Gettysburg to the Rapidan; it relies on Meade's, Hancock's, Warren's, Burnside's, Parke's and Wilson's reports and quotes Lee's, Beauregard's and Gordon's despatches, so it is not independent of those families. Gillmore's, Meade's, Hancock's, Burnside's, Wilson's, Hampton's, Stannard's and Lee's papers, printed in Official Records Series I, Volumes XXXVI (Part 2), XL, XLII and XLVI (Part 1), are separate families of interested commanders' accounts; each volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Lee's telegrams largely relay subordinates' reports. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
